newsitem.title: USA: Jacksonville, Fla, Electric takes over water-sewer.
newsitem.headline: Jacksonville, Fla, Electric takes over water-sewer.

text.p: Florida's Jacksonville City Council has turned over management of the city water and sewer department to Jacksonville Electric Authority .
The move was approved Tuesday night and transfers debt service responsibility for water-sewer bonds to the electric authority, city Treasurer Richard Cohee said Wednesday.
"They will receive revenues and continue to make debt service payments. In the future, the JEA would issue water and sewer debt," Cohee said.
In exchange for the water-sewer department, with assets valued at $250 million, the electric authority will pay the city $9 million annually as a contribution in lieu of taxes.
"We are giving them the utility. They are giving us back what you might call a dividend," Cohee said.
That $9 million annual revenue stream will be pledged to repay a city bond issue of about $70 million for stormwater drainage projects, with the city retains jurisdiction over.
The issue is planned for late December, with PaineWebber as senior manager.

The utility merger is expected to save the city up to $9 million a year through increased productivity, lower overtime expenses, reduced borrowing costs and greater interest on investments. By using that savings to back the stormwater bonds, the city avoids a potential new tax for its stormwater program.

The water and sewer department's 700 employees do not face layoffs, but the electric authority has the option of offering a one-time voluntary severance package if it finds employees performing duplicate tasks.

The city council retains some control because it approves the authority's annual budget and still must approve water-sewer projects. But it gave up authority to set water and sewer rates, which will be set by the electric authority's appointed board. As part of the deal, consumers were promised a five-year freeze on water-sewer rates.
Utility bills will continue to come on separate statements but eventually could be consolidated.
Cohee said the move was not expected to affect the city's credit standing. Jacksonville general obligation bonds are rated Aa by Moody's Investors and AA by Standard & Poor's and Fitch Investors.

But it is expected to reduce borrowing costs for future water-sewer projects because the electric authority's revenue bonds are rated higher than the city's GOs by two of the three agencies -- AA1 by Moody's and AA-plus by Fitch.
The name of the electic utility, which enjoys a sterling reputation in the bond markets, remains unchanged.

"They are still to me, the best operating utility in the United States. JEA operates pretty lean and efficient for a public entity," said Doug Byrne, a fund manager for Barnett Banks Inc. "It's a great credit."
Barnett holds JEA bonds in its individual and common trust funds, and sometimes in its Emerald Florida Tax-Free fund.
